spans.s:
1. Vayas is a common name for ‘bird’ in the Atharvaveda and later.
Foot notes iii. 21, 2; vi. 59, 1; vii. 96, 1; viii. 7, 24, etc.
taittirīya Saṃhitā, iii. 1, 1, 1; v. 2, 5, 1; 5, 3, 2. etc.

2. Vayas denotes in the Atharvaveda and later the ‘age of animals or men.’
Foot notes xii. 3, 1.
kāṭhaka Saṃhitā, xi. 2; taittirīya brāhmaṇa, iii. 12, 5, 9; Śatapatha brāhmaṇa, iii. 1, 2, 21; 3, 3, 3. etc.

Vayā in the Rigveda denotes the ‘branch’ of a tree.
Foot notes ii. 5, 4; v. 1, 1; vi. 7, 6; 13, 1; viii. 13, 6, 17, etc.

Vayya occurs in several passages of the Rigveda in connexion with turvīti, of whom the word is, according to Sāyaṇa, a patronymic in one passage. Roth is inclined to think that the sense of ‘companion’ would suit all passages.
Foot notes i. 54, 6; 112, 6 (where turvīti does not occur); ii. 13, 12; iv. 19, 6.
On Rv. i. 54, 6.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v., quoting ix. 68, 8, as a clear case.
Vāyya, ‘descendant of vayya,’ is the patronymic of satyaśravas in the Rigveda (v. 79, 1. 2).
Vayitrī in the pañcaviṃśa brāhmaṇa (i. 8, 9) denotes a ‘female weaver.’
Vāyata, ‘descendant of Vayant,’ is the patronymic of Pāśadyumna in the Rigveda (vii. 33, 2). Cf. Vyant.

Vāyasa in the Rigveda and later denotes a ‘large bird.’ The sense of ‘crow’ occurs in the Ṣaḍviṃśa brāhmaṇa only.
Foot notes i. 164, 32.
In a Vedic citation in nirukta, iv. 17; and in verse 1 of khila after Rv. v. 51.
The only sense of the word in the post-Vedic language.
vi. 8.

Vāyo-vidyika, ‘bird-catcher,’ is found in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes xiii. 4, 3, 13. Cf. Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East, 44, 369, n. 5.
